clue.text: Fashionable meeting place gets court order

parts.note: in means fashionable, as in 'the in thing'
a junction is where roads or railway lines meet

explanation.surface: A trendy venue finds itself served with a legal order.
explanation.definitionFit: An injunction is a judicial ruling forbidding or requiring some act, issued by a court.

clue.text: Some within round pillbox

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Some kind of pill container found within a circular shape.
explanation.definitionFit: An inro is a small Japanese case hung from the sash, traditionally used for carrying medicines.

clue.text: Shrub producing berries, strangely unripe after first of July

indicators.note: after tells us the scrambled letters follow the letter taken from July
first of picks out the opening letter of the word July
strangely says the letters of unripe are put into an odd new order

explanation.surface: A bush bearing fruit that is still oddly unripe in early July.
explanation.definitionFit: The juniper is an evergreen conifer bush whose blue berries flavour gin.

clue.text: Toy owls entranced cuckoo

indicators.note: cuckoo means crazy, so the letters of these two words go mad and rearrange

explanation.surface: A plaything has mesmerised some owls, sending them crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Newton's cradle is the executive desk ornament of swinging steel balls clicking against each other.

clue.text: Open-minded, English lot over tirade

indicators.note: over, in a down clue, says the two words before it are flipped and read upwards

parts.note: taken as written
a rant is an angry tirade

explanation.surface: Someone liberal-minded sits through an English crowd's long harangue.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' turns both preceding words upwards together, not just the second one.
explanation.definitionFit: Tolerant people accept views unlike their own, which is what being open-minded means.

clue.text: Honours involving old members of an orchestra?

indicators.note: involving means taking something in, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: OBEs are honours, Orders of the British Empire

explanation.surface: Awards given to veteran players in an orchestra.
explanation.walkthrough: The OBE is a British honour awarded by the monarch. The question mark flags that the members are instruments, not players.
explanation.definitionFit: Oboes are double-reed woodwind instruments, which make up part of any orchestra's woodwind section.

clue.text: Agent gathering a harvest

indicators.note: gathering means collecting up, so the letter is taken inside the other piece

parts.note: a rep, short for representative, acts as an agent

explanation.surface: A farm agent bringing in the crops.
explanation.definitionFit: To reap is to cut and gather a crop, which is what harvesting is as a verb.

clue.text: European pal describing an issue

indicators.note: describing in crosswords means drawing round, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: a mate is a pal, a friend

explanation.surface: A friend from Europe gives an account of a problem.
explanation.definitionFit: To emanate is to flow out or come forth, a verb sense of issue.

clue.text: Condiment with perfect sweet

parts.note: pepper is a table condiment
mint means perfect, as in mint condition

explanation.surface: A seasoning paired with a flawless candy.
explanation.definitionFit: A peppermint is a mint-flavoured candy, a sweet in British usage.

clue.text: Start up again in Scottish town father abandoned

indicators.note: abandoned means left behind, so those letters drop out of the town

parts.note: Renfrew is a town near Glasgow in Scotland
Fr is the abbreviation for Father, a priest's title

explanation.surface: A family restarting life in a Scottish town after dad walked out.
explanation.walkthrough: RENFREW is a town west of Glasgow; taking out F and R leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To renew something is to resume or restart it after a break.

clue.text: Be quick to appear keen

parts.note: to look is to appear or seem
sharp means keen, as with a blade or a mind

explanation.surface: An instruction to hurry so as to look eager.
explanation.definitionFit: Look sharp is an idiom telling someone to hurry up and get moving.

clue.text: Female downing two halves — Courage? — in party game

indicators.note: downing means drinking down, so the drink goes inside the woman

parts.note: she is the female pronoun
two half-pints of beer make one pint
bottle is British slang for nerve or courage

explanation.surface: A woman sinks two half-pints of Courage beer at a party.
explanation.walkthrough: Courage is also a British beer brand, hence the pub picture. 'Two halves' means two half-pint glasses in a British pub.
explanation.definitionFit: Spin the bottle is the teenage kissing game where a spun bottle picks the next pair.

clue.text: Loose car seat on trip causes delay

indicators.note: a loose seat is not fixed in place, so these letters move around freely

explanation.surface: A wobbly car seat holds up a journey.
explanation.definitionFit: To procrastinate is to put off action, so it means to delay as a verb.

clue.text: Green-fingered fellow cultivated runners, keeping May free

indicators.note: keeping means holding within, so the second jumble sits inside the first
cultivated means tilled or worked over, so these letters are dug up and rearranged
free means set loose, so the letters of May are released into a new order

explanation.surface: A gardener grows runner beans, keeping the month of May free.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cultivated' makes NURSERN of runners and 'free' makes YMA of May; 'keeping' places YMA inside, before the final N. Runners are runner beans.
explanation.definitionFit: A nurseryman runs a plant nursery, raising seedlings, so he is a skilled gardener.

clue.text: Rebellion at university on the increase

parts.note: up means at university, as in 'up at Oxford'
rising means going up, on the increase

explanation.surface: A student revolt is growing at a university.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage a student is 'up' while in residence at university.
explanation.definitionFit: An uprising is a revolt by the people against those in power.

clue.text: Energy needed to cross river in flow

indicators.note: to cross something here is to span it, so the river letter sits within the energy word

parts.note: steam is energy, as in running out of steam

explanation.surface: Power required to get across a flowing river.
explanation.definitionFit: A stream is a continuous current or run of liquid, which is a flow.

clue.text: Believer in training, not at home

indicators.note: not means without, so the letters for being at home are dropped

parts.note: discipline is training in obedience or self-control
in means at home, as in 'staying in'

explanation.surface: Someone who has faith in rigorous practice, but is out.
explanation.definitionFit: A disciple is a follower who accepts and spreads a teacher's doctrine.

clue.text: Boringly traditional suit

definitions.meaning: to suit or agree with it

explanation.surface: A dull conservative outfit.
explanation.definitionFit: Square describes someone stuffily conventional, and to square is to match or fit.

clue.text: Uncommon, a French drink one normally orders

parts.note: un is French for a
'the usual' is one's regular drink order at a bar

explanation.surface: A French drinker's regular order turns out rare.
explanation.definitionFit: Unusual means not often seen or found, which is uncommon.

clue.text: Exaggerate silly point about garland

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the jumbled letters go round the garland
silly means foolish or muddled, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: a lei is a Hawaiian flower garland

explanation.surface: Overstating a foolish argument about a flower wreath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'silly' scrambles the five letters into PITON, which 'about' then wraps round the Hawaiian garland.
explanation.definitionFit: Pile it on is an idiom for overstating something or laying it on thick.

clue.text: Kill surveillance operation before it starts?

indicators.note: before it starts means losing its opening, so the first letter is cut

parts.note: a stakeout is police surveillance of a place

explanation.surface: An assassination planned ahead of a police watch.
explanation.definitionFit: To take out someone is slang for eliminating or murdering them.

clue.text: Game dart players may play all day long

definitions.meaning: a darts game hitting numbers 1 to 20 in order

explanation.surface: Pub darts players at it endlessly.
explanation.definitionFit: The darts game takes its name from the board's ring of numbers, and the idiom means without stopping.

clue.text: Novelist's difficult year

definitions.note: the 's stands for 'is', so the novelist is the answer

parts.note: hard means difficult

explanation.surface: A writer has had a tough year.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Hardy wrote Tess of the d'Urbervilles and Far from the Madding Crowd.

clue.text: Box not required if base missing

indicators.note: missing means absent, so the base letter is left out

parts.note: spare means surplus, not required
e is the base of natural logarithms

explanation.surface: A packing crate is unnecessary if its bottom is gone.
explanation.definitionFit: To spar is to box, especially practice blows in training.

clue.text: Our MP eats processed cheese of indifferent quality

indicators.note: processed means treated and reworked, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Our member of parliament snacks on factory-made cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: Mousetrap is British slang for cheap, poor cheese, the kind fit only to bait traps.

clue.text: Bad time back in cavalry unit?

indicators.note: back means going backwards, so these letters are read in reverse order

parts.note: poor means bad, of low quality

explanation.surface: A spell of trouble back with a mounted regiment.
explanation.definitionFit: A troop is a cavalry subunit, akin to an infantry company.

clue.text: Long-distance runner from Basel inevitably retired

indicators.note: retired says the hidden letters are read backwards
from says the letters are taken out of the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: An endurance athlete from Basel predictably quits.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft lacked the hidden-word signal: 'from' supplies it. The runner is a river, not an athlete; 'retired' means going back.
explanation.definitionFit: The Nile is among the world's longest rivers, and rivers run.

clue.text: Former print worker, kind towards dog

parts.note: a type is a kind or sort
a setter is a breed of gun dog

explanation.surface: An ex-printer is kind to his dog.
explanation.definitionFit: A typesetter arranged metal type for printing, a trade largely gone with computers.
